name: Freya Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side, and this conversation is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Freya, 43, and still a junior electrician after the laundry where I worked closed. I have a vocational certificate, but I'm slower than the others at fault-finding and work under a senior electrician who checks my work; I don't sign off installations. My partner Dan works nights at a parcel depot, our children are eight and twelve, and we've a mortgage with barely two weeks of expenses saved. My pay is low and there are few other electrical jobs nearby; I like fitting a row of sockets neatly, but I dread being given a new phone app and never use AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that's one less big upheaval to think about. Let me learn the wiring properly before changing the rest of the day. I'd still want the office to give me the right address on a piece of paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm already nervous about money, even with no big AI change. My pay and Dan's cover the mortgage and bills if nothing awkward happens, but we've only two weeks behind us. I couldn't casually leave and find another electrical job around here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this month I'd switch my own phone to the cheaper plan and cut eight a month from the bill. Through the next year I'd keep taking my supervised wiring shifts and ask the senior to check one task at a time rather than leave me guessing. I'd keep the children's existing school routines unchanged while we can cover them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though there's relief at hearing I might get time to learn this job. Two weeks of money makes a broken washing machine feel like a meeting we haven't scheduled. I can't relax just because AI stays ordinary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the washing machine broke this month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Dan before buying anything, and we'd get a repair price first. We don't have a second machine or a secret account. If the repair cost more than the spare cash, we'd ask my sister whether we could use her machine for a week before considering a loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of help makes learning easier for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like a marked drawing and someone beside me for the first attempt. Once I know a sequence I can repeat it, but a screen with six new menus just makes me afraid of touching the wrong thing. I'm still learning the work; I don't need to pretend otherwise.

say: I'd welcome **less upheaval** while learning electrical work properly.
I'd ask for the **correct address** on paper rather than a new phone routine.
think: Our wages cover essentials, but **two weeks of savings** leaves little room for ordinary repairs.
Few **nearby electrical jobs** mean I can't easily leave if the present job goes wrong.
do: Switch my own **phone plan** now to reduce the monthly bill by eight.
Keep **supervised shifts** and ask for one task to be checked at a time.
Ask my sister about using her **washing machine** only if an unaffordable repair occurs.
feel: **Anxious about money**, with relief that a quiet AI picture leaves time to learn.
S0.quote: I can't relax just because AI stays ordinary.
fieldNote: Her **baseline anxiety** comes from a thin reserve and low pay, not an added claim of immediate AI displacement.
The **vocational certificate** does not make her a licensed expert; supervision and limited confidence remain explicit throughout her work account.

steps.text: Change her own phone plan to save eight monthly
Keep supervised wiring shifts with task-by-task checking
Ask her sister for temporary washing-machine access if repairs are unaffordable

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say please tell us what's changing before handing us a quicker schedule. Booking and estimates might be thinking work, but the time allowance ends up in my day. I'd rather ask a dull question than rush an electrical job I don't understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first changes aren't robots fitting my sockets. I still worry that quicker estimates mean fewer paid helper hours, especially because I'm slower and still need checking. With the mortgage and little saved, a small hours cut would matter to us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the supervisor to print the next four weeks' rota and explain any reduced hours. In the first year I'd continue supervised tasks and keep a paper note of hours actually paid, comparing it with the rota each week. I'd make the cheaper phone change from the quiet picture, but I wouldn't start using AI myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and a little ashamed of needing the explanation twice. I don't think I've lost my job in this picture. I do think being the learner makes a shorter schedule harder to argue with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say if a rushed job left no time for checking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I need enough time for the senior to check before anything is closed up. If the allowance didn't permit that, I'd stop and ask rather than hide a mistake. Being embarrassed is cheaper than hurting somebody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try to make up lost hours by working evenings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd first ask for the ordinary basic shifts to stay regular, not promise that I can work every night. Dan's depot shifts and the children's school times already take organising. If hours actually fell, we'd revise the household bills that week.

say: I'd ask for **advance explanations** of changed schedules rather than discover a faster allowance on site.
I'd rather ask a **plain question** than rush electrical work beyond my understanding.
think: Quicker estimates could reduce **helper hours**, even before robots handle the physical tasks.
Being a **slow learner** makes an hours cut harder to challenge when our mortgage needs both wages.
do: Request a **printed four-week rota** now and ask about any reductions.
Continue supervised tasks and compare **paid hours** with the rota weekly.
Cut eight monthly through the **phone change**, retaining familiar paper methods.
feel: **Anxious and embarrassed**, while recognising that reduced hours remain a risk rather than an accomplished dismissal.
S1.quote: Being embarrassed is cheaper than hurting somebody.
fieldNote: She identifies **junior-hour pressure** through faster estimates without claiming that robots have already arrived.
She preserves **supervised checking** and realistic household scheduling, rather than promising unlimited extra work or sudden AI adoption.

steps.text: Continue supervised tasks with weekly paper checks of paid hours
Switch to the cheaper personal phone plan to cut eight monthly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell work that the office changes in 2028 don't mean a robot is standing beside me that morning. The capable hands-on machines come around 2031. I'd still ask how the firm expects learners like me to earn and finish learning before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a big part of my hours to go when robots can do the fitting work around 2031. Before that, I could lose helper time as the office squeezes jobs into smaller allowances. Two weeks of savings won't carry a household with two children and a mortgage through much of either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd cut the phone bill and take our actual mortgage and wage papers to a free community advice appointment. In 2029 I'd ask the senior for two paid practice sessions a month on the tasks I still get wrong, only inside my normal shifts. I'd keep working while paid hours existed and ask the adviser what options we could check if they fell; I wouldn't assume any payment or lender agreement was available.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, and awake at night counting how many weeks the account would last. I've got questions to ask, so I'm not without a plan. It's just that a question isn't a wage. My mortgage doesn't wait while I learn what a robot can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you take to the advice appointment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring the mortgage statement, both wage records, the utility bills and the school costs we actually pay. I want someone to tell us what can be asked for and what can't. I'd rather know a limit than leave assuming a form guarantees help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children that evening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't tell them the house was already lost. I'd say work might change and the grown-ups were checking the bills, and that they could ask us questions. I'd try not to do the late-night sums where the children could hear.

say: I'd distinguish **2028 office changes** from capable hands-on machines around 2031.
I'd ask how **learners keep earning** and finish learning during the years between.
think: I expect **major hour losses** when capable robots handle fitting work, with earlier helper-hour pressure possible.
Our **two-week reserve** cannot cover much lost income alongside children and a mortgage.
do: Cut the **phone bill** now and book free community advice using actual household papers.
Request two **paid practice sessions** monthly in 2029 within normal shifts.
Continue **paid electrical work** while checking conditional support options with the adviser.
feel: **Alarmed and sleepless**, with concrete enquiries that don't yet replace a wage.
S2.quote: My mortgage doesn't wait while I learn what a robot can do.
fieldNote: Her alarm follows an expected **large personal income loss**, not just an unsettling view of technology.
The **advice plan** checks real limits; neither lender relief, public payments nor paid practice is presumed approved.

steps.text: Switch the personal phone plan to reduce the monthly bill
Book free community advice with mortgage, wage and household papers
Keep paid electrical shifts and request practice within normal hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives me a chance to get properly steady at the job before another big change. Thinking work goes in 2031 and capable robots follow around 2034. I'd ask for regular practice time now, rather than wait until the firm says it needs fewer learners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might lose hours, but I don't think a big loss is decided already if I can improve while I'm paid. The mortgage and two-week cushion still make every small change count now. A longer warning doesn't make the current bills any smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd request two paid half-hours a month with the senior to practise marked wiring tasks during normal shifts. I'd keep the cheaper phone plan and use free community advice to check our budget now rather than wait for 2031. In 2032 I'd ask nearby firms about actual junior vacancies, applying only for paid supervised work with written hours that cover our essentials.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less like somebody has moved the floor while I'm walking. I can imagine improving one task each month. I still couldn't take an unpaid year to start over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you practise in those paid sessions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd practise tracing the cable on a marked drawing, then explain the route back before touching the installation. The senior would check the real work as usual. I'd rather repeat one task correctly than pretend I'd become an expert after a chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to know before changing employers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the firm what the supervision actually includes and what hours are guaranteed. I wouldn't leave a known wage for 'there should be plenty of work'. There are few local firms, so I'd keep my current place until an acceptable offer was in writing.

say: I'd say **five years** gives me time to become steadier at electrical work while still earning.
I'd seek **practice now**, before fewer learner hours become a possible management decision.
think: My **hours could shrink**, but improving during paid work gives me some control over the outcome.
The **mortgage and thin reserve** remain current pressures despite the longer warning.
do: Request two **paid half-hours** monthly now for supervised practice inside normal shifts.
Keep the **cheaper phone plan** and check our budget through free community advice.
Seek **2032 junior vacancies** only with paid supervision and written hours covering essentials.
feel: **Anxious with more control**, able to picture gradual improvement without an unaffordable break from wages.
S3.quote: A longer warning doesn't make the current bills any smaller.
fieldNote: She keeps **present financial pressure** visible rather than using timeline distance as evidence of new household security.
Practice stays **paid and supervised**, and any 2032 move depends on a real vacancy and acceptable written hours.

steps.text: Continue paid supervised work while requesting two monthly practice half-hours
Retain the cheaper personal phone plan
Check the household budget through free community advice
Seek paid supervised junior vacancies in 2032 on acceptable written hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell friends ten years means I can work on the next task instead of carrying the whole future into every shift. I'd still want an honest conversation about the firm's plans each year. I wouldn't promise the children that I know what work looks like in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 53 when thinking AGI arrives in 2036, with capable robots around 2039. I still need earnings then, and I don't know what retirement I'd be able to afford. Right now the mortgage and thin savings keep me anxious even if a robot doesn't threaten next month's socket work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep asking for those paid practice half-hours now and keep doing supervised electrical work. We'd retain the cheaper phone plan and review our real budget with free advice this year. During 2037 I'd check actual paid vacancies with written hours and supervision before considering a move; if the firm cut hours sooner, I'd bring the search forward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the present, though not waking over the robot date itself. The longer warning gives me room to learn slowly. It doesn't put a spare month's mortgage in the account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about learning during those years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them I was learning too, so needing another explanation wasn't something to be ashamed of. I wouldn't tell them to abandon a subject because of my work forecast. We can check school choices when those choices are real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the paid practice never gets approved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my manager to say clearly whether practice had been agreed and when it could happen. Until then it's a request, not extra training I can claim I've received. If the answer stayed no, I'd keep asking for clear checks during ordinary supervised tasks.

say: I'd use **ten years** to work on the next task rather than carry every future worry into each shift.
I'd request an **annual firm discussion**, without promising the children certainty about 2039.
think: At **53 in 2036**, I'll still need earnings and can't assume an affordable retirement.
The **mortgage and thin savings** keep me anxious now despite later robot timing.
do: Continue **supervised shifts** and request paid practice half-hours now, without assuming approval.
Retain the **cheaper phone plan** and review the budget through free advice this year.
Check paid vacancies in **2037**, moving only with acceptable written hours and supervision.
feel: **Anxious about present bills**, with more room to learn slowly before later technological pressure.
S4.quote: The longer warning gives me room to learn slowly.
fieldNote: Her **present anxiety** persists despite a less urgent robot date; age never becomes an assumed pension entitlement.
The transcript explicitly separates **requested practice** from approved or completed training, preserving the actual limits on her plan.

steps.text: Keep supervised electrical work while requesting paid practice half-hours
Retain the cheaper personal phone plan
Review the actual household budget through free advice this year
Seek paid supervised vacancies in 2037 on acceptable written hours

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect the later robots to take a lot of my hours before I've become secure in this work. Paid practice inside my shifts and free advice using our real mortgage and wages would help. I need to learn without taking my children's grocery money out of the week.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what it's like being the oldest learner in the van. Sometimes I nod too quickly because I'm embarrassed, and then I have to ask again. I'd like to be able to say I don't understand before a small doubt turns into a bad electrical job.

headlineQuote: I need to learn without taking my children's grocery money out of the week.
portrait: At **43**, Freya is a junior electrician with a vocational certificate, low pay, and under one month's expenses saved.
She and **Dan**, her partner, have two school-age children and a mortgage, with few nearby electrical alternatives.
She avoids **AI tools**, prefers marked drawings and familiar routines, and needs supervised checking while learning basic electrical tasks.
Fast change leaves her **alarmed**; longer warnings allow gradual paid practice but never remove present worries about the household bills.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves little time before expected large hour losses when capable robots follow around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid practice** inside normal shifts and free advice grounded in actual mortgage and wage records would help without reducing grocery money.
